title: We’re addicted to locking people up—but it doesn’t make us safer
gist: England and Wales face a hard capacity wall in the prison system — no space for new offenders by November — driven not by one failure but by ministerial churn (13 prison ministers in ten years), a collapsed probation service recalling 40,000 people a year, three decades of sentence inflation, and a Ministry of Justice day-to-day budget set to run 14 per cent below its 2007/08 level. The test set for new PM Andy Burnham is whether he will apply his promised 'circuit-breaker' to the whole criminal justice chain rather than the prison estate alone.

insights.claim: England and Wales have had 13 prison ministers in the past ten years — an average tenure of about nine months — and ten justice secretaries over the same period, averaging one year each.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Nine-month average tenure makes multi-year capital programmes and probation reform structurally undeliverable — discount any announced UK justice reform timeline that assumes a stable sponsor minister.
insights.quote: In the past ten years there have been no fewer than 13 prison ministers.

insights.claim: James Timpson, appointed prisons minister by Keir Starmer, resigned after 24 months just days before the latest early-release controversy engulfed his former department, and was by most accounts ineffective despite being an imaginative appointment.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Bringing in an outside operator with sector credibility did not move the system — evidence that the constraint is structural and fiscal, not managerial talent.

insights.claim: The newly appointed justice secretary Alex Norris is not a lawyer and came from a career as an East Midlands area organiser for Unison and a Nottingham city councillor for the Basford ward, following the precedents of non-lawyers Chris Grayling and Liz Truss in the role.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A politically lightweight appointment to a portfolio in crisis signals the government is not yet treating justice as a first-order priority.
insights.locator: But don’t worry, because we have a new justice secretary

themes.theme: Hard capacity wall and the estate build shortfall

insights.claim: Dangerous criminals are being released early because prisons in England and Wales are at bursting point and by November there will be nowhere to put new offenders.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A dated capacity cliff in November is a forced-policy catalyst: expect emergency release schemes, sentencing legislation or court-listing changes rather than orderly reform.
insights.locator: Why are we releasing dangerous criminals back onto the streets?

insights.claim: Over 14 years in power the Conservatives expanded the prison estate by fewer than 500 places, while the Starmer government's claimed 2,500 additional places came mostly from a prison-building programme the Conservatives had started.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Two decades of near-zero net capacity addition against rising sentence lengths means the shortfall cannot be built out within a parliament — the adjustment must come from sentencing or remand policy.
insights.locator: After 14 years in power the Tories

insights.claim: Prisoners in England and Wales are held in cells for up to 22 hours a day at a cost of £58,000 per head, roughly equivalent to fees at exclusive private schools such as Uppingham, with essentially no education or rehabilitation delivered in return.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: £58k a head for warehousing with no rehabilitation output is the strongest available fiscal argument for sentencing reform — the cost-per-place figure is the number that moves Treasury opinion.
insights.locator: We sling convicts in cells for up to 22 hours a day

insights.claim: England and Wales incarcerate twice the proportion of the population that Germany does and three times that of the Netherlands, Norway or Finland.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The international comparison sets the scale of the potential policy swing: converging even part-way toward German rates would transform prison capital and operating budgets.
insights.locator: Have we ever stopped to wonder why

themes.theme: Recall and the broken probation service

insights.claim: Around 40,000 ex-convicts a year are currently being recalled to prison in England and Wales, with 13,000 to 15,000 people held on recall at any one time, compared with fewer than 100 in the early 1990s.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Recall alone now consumes a prison population that barely existed 30 years ago — reforming recall rules is the fastest available lever to free capacity without new building.
insights.locator: If we had a properly functioning probation service

insights.claim: Chris Grayling's dramatic reform of the probation service just over ten years ago failed on every single count, and is a direct contributor to today's recall-driven overcrowding.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A cautionary precedent for outsourcing-led justice reform: the probation privatisation is the reference case cited against similar structural experiments.
insights.locator: So let’s not forget to blame Chris Grayling

themes.theme: Sentence inflation and the mechanism driving it

insights.claim: Average custodial sentences in England and Wales have risen from 16 months in 1993 to 22 months today, and the typical term for murder has gone from 12 years to 21 years — the driver of demand that David Gauke's review documented as sentence inflation.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Population growth is coming from length-of-stay, not offence volume — meaning capacity forecasts are locked in for decades unless tariffs change.
insights.locator: In 1993 we locked people up for 16 months on average

insights.claim: Judges are not the cause of longer sentences — they apply what the law obliges — so the causal chain runs back to politicians who keep ramping up statutory sentences in response to perceived public pressure.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Any durable fix requires primary legislation on sentencing, not judicial guidance — so watch the legislative timetable, not the Sentencing Council.
insights.locator: But the judges are only doing what the law obliges them to do

insights.claim: David Gauke partly blames the media's persistent 'tough on crime' narrative for convincing the public that British jails are soft, a framing Chris Grayling captured in describing them as 'like holiday camps'.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The political constraint on reform is a media narrative, not measured public opinion — so a change in press framing is the leading indicator that reform has become possible.
insights.locator: Well, Gauke partly blames the media

themes.theme: Public opinion is misread by politicians

insights.claim: More than three quarters of the public in England and Wales believe sentencing has become shorter, when the opposite is true — so MPs are responding to a factually inverted perception of their own record.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The 'public demands toughness' assumption underpinning UK sentencing policy rests on a measurement error — a correctable one, which makes reform more politically feasible than assumed.
insights.quote: we’re not soft on offenders, but the public thinks we are
insights.locator: More than three quarters of us believe

insights.claim: Public opinion on prisons is more nuanced than the toughness narrative implies: people do think violent offenders should be locked up, but 75 per cent believe the prison system is failing.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: There is a 75 per cent mandate for 'the system is broken' framing — political cover exists for reform pitched as effectiveness rather than leniency.
insights.locator: However, public opinion is also much more nuanced

themes.theme: Courts crisis and the fiscal squeeze

insights.claim: Two reports from Lord Leveson warn that the court system in England and Wales is so catastrophically degraded that aspects of the jury system may have to be abandoned to keep it functioning, with some serious offences not heard until 2030.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Constitutional-scale change to jury trial is now on the table as a capacity measure — a live legislative fight to watch, with knock-ons for legal services and remand populations.
insights.locator: Two blockbuster reports from Lord Leveson

insights.claim: Four-year waits for trial mean defendants can sit on remand at a cost to the taxpayer of over £50,000 a year while the Ministry of Justice's real day-to-day budget is set to be 14 per cent lower than in 2007/08.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A department running 14 per cent below its 2007/08 real budget while unit costs exceed £50k a head is the arithmetic behind the collapse — the deficit must be closed by spending, sentencing or procedure.
insights.quote: the real day-to-day budget of the Ministry of Justice is set to be 14 per cent lower than in 2007/08
insights.locator: As Leveson notes, the real day-to-day budget

themes.theme: Framing the fix: taps versus bath

insights.claim: The right mental model for the prisons crisis is that the country is scrambling to empty the bath at the bottom while both the hot and cold taps gush at the top — capacity relief without upstream sentencing and court reform cannot work.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Judge announced reforms by whether they touch inflow (sentencing, recall, court throughput) rather than outflow (early release) — outflow-only measures will recur every few months.
insights.quote: We are currently scrambling to empty the bath at the bottom while both hot and cold taps are gushing away at the top.
insights.locator: Have we ever stopped to wonder why

insights.claim: The underlying national error is the belief that locking up more people for longer solves anything, an addiction that no amount of estate expansion can offset.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The author's frame implies sustained upward pressure on justice spending unless a political leader breaks the sentencing consensus — a persistent fiscal liability line.
insights.quote: we are addicted to the pathetically deluded idea that by locking up more and more people for ever lengthier periods of time, we are solving anything
insights.locator: But the bigger problems lie further up the food chain

insights.claim: Andy Burnham entered Downing Street conceding that politicians had not been good enough and promising a 'circuit-breaker', and the criminal justice system is the part of government most in need of one — but his willingness to spend political capital on it is unproven.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Whether Burnham owns justice reform personally is the single variable that determines if the November capacity wall triggers reform or another emergency release round.
insights.quote: He has the vibes. Does he have the attention span, the will and the courage?
insights.locator: When Andy Burnham walked into Downing Street
